question: the steady real-time factor fell from 0.9588 to 0.8669 across six runs in 75 minutes. What limits it, and what was falling?

cache_experiment.design: ABA on ground_material.cache_slots, 32 -> 128 -> 32, four tracks over 100 m at the rated speed on one seed. The outer arms bound the drift, which is the whole reason the middle arm cannot be read on its own.

arms.name: cache_a32
arms.when: before the WSL restart, after three full-area runs and a heavy audit pass

cache_experiment.verdict: null. Raising the cache fourfold changed the real-time factor by 0.0001 once drift is removed, and changed the tile counts not at all: 3392/3390/3389 loads and 3368/3367/3366 evictions.
cache_experiment.mechanism: eviction is not capacity driven. prefetch_ahead_m 1.5 and prefetch_behind_m 0.5 bound the working set, so a tile is generated once as the camera sweeps over it and dropped when the window moves on. Four 100 m tracks sweep about 3900 tiles and the run loads 3390: each tile is paid for once. Holding them instead would need the whole x range of a y band -- thousands of slots at about 38.6 MB each -- so the streaming cost is structural, not a tuning mistake.
cache_experiment.correction: the 8455 evictions in the earlier full-area run were read as cache thrash. They are not; they are streaming.

degradation.observation: steady RTF by run, in order, over 75 minutes: 0.9588, 0.9450, 0.9439 (ten tracks), 0.9060, 0.8866, 0.8669 (four tracks)
degradation.within_run: RTF measured in 60 s windows shows no downward trend inside any run; the whole distribution sits lower for each successive launch. The level is set at process start, not accumulated during the run.

ruled_out.our_processes: every run is a fresh process tree and no process survives between runs, so a leak in our code cannot carry over. Peak RSS and device memory were flat across runs.
ruled_out.gpu_thermal: the GPU sat idle for about 25 minutes between run 3 and run 4 while a CPU and disk bound audit ran, and RTF still fell from 0.9439 to 0.9060. During the clean run it peaked at 56 C.
ruled_out.host_exhaustion: 12 GB of host memory and 854 GB of disk were free at the worst point; no stray processes.
ruled_out.dxg_ioctl_failures: counted 0 in one early run and 600-900 in later ones, which looked like a lead. It is not: the clean post-restart run logged 598 of them and had the best RTF of any four-track arm.

decisive_test.action: wsl --shutdown from Windows, then rerun the identical four-track arm at 32 slots on the same seed
decisive_test.verdict: the degradation is state accumulated outside our processes in the WSL or host GPU stack, and a WSL restart clears it. It also cleared the page cache, so restart-clears-it is established while which of the two mattered is not.

degradation.consequence: a real-time factor measured without recording how long WSL has been up, and how many simulations have run in it, is not comparable to another. The three repeat-run figures were runs one to three after roughly two and a half hours of uptime, so they are lower bounds rather than the configuration.

what_limits_it.gpu_reading: median utilization 32 percent, median memory bandwidth 10 percent, median power 95 W of a 360 W limit, clocks at boost and 51 C. The GPU is idle about two thirds of the time.
what_limits_it.cpu_reading: 24 cores with a load average near 5.6 during the run, about 23 percent of the machine.
what_limits_it.work_is_fixed_by_area: line spacing is 0.3662 mm in space, so 100 x 10 m is 2.88 M lines and 8.64 M renders whether the vehicle drives 2.0 or 2.78 m/s. The rated run rendered 86.7 s and the 2 m/s run 97.0 s for the same area. Going faster adds no pixels; it gives the simulator fewer simulated seconds to hide the same work in, which is why RTF falls with speed by construction.
what_limits_it.interpretation: latency and serialisation bound, not throughput bound: 8.64 M launches of about 10 us each, against a single threaded 1 ms physics step that the mission needs 761000 of. Neither more cores nor a larger GPU would move it; fewer and larger submissions would.

not_covered: which of the two things a WSL restart clears -- host GPU stack state or page cache -- is responsible
whether RTF keeps degrading within a fresh WSL at the same rate, and after how many runs it crosses a floor
a repeat of the three full-area acceptance runs from a fresh WSL, which is what a comparable RTF figure would need
